channel.title: Oddly Wired
channel.description: One checked psychology fact a day. Every claim names the study behind it.

item.title: Your eye movements reflect your internal search patterns.
item.description: Visual search time increases linearly with set size specifically during serial (conjunction) search, whereas feature search is conducted in parallel with a near-zero slope.

item.title: You repeat a story until the details disappear.
item.description: A classic study showed that when participants retold a story over several sessions, they consistently simplified the narrative and discarded unconventional details.

item.title: Time perception changes as you get older.
item.description: Research indicates that your sense of how fast time passes is linked to how much new information you encode; as encoding slows, time feels like it accelerates.

item.title: You subconsciously shift your persona for every setting.
item.description: Individuals who score high in self-monitoring intentionally adjust their behavior to match the expectations of their immediate social environment.

item.title: Curiosity is the physical feeling of a missing piece.
item.description: A 1994 analysis defined curiosity as a 'cognitively induced deprivation' triggered by the awareness of a gap in one's knowledge.

item.title: Remembering to remember is a distinct, fragile process.
item.description: Research shows that prospective memory—the ability to perform a future intention—relies on different brain mechanisms than retrospective memory.

item.title: Your language shapes how your brain perceives color.
item.description: A 2007 study showed that Russian speakers, who have distinct words for light and dark blue, could categorize these colors faster than English speakers.

item.title: High visual focus can render you temporarily deaf.
item.description: A 2011 study found that participants focused on a difficult visual task failed to hear a distinct tone played repeatedly in their ears.

item.title: Describing a face makes you worse at identifying it.
item.description: A 1990 study found that participants who wrote a verbal description of a face were significantly less likely to correctly pick it out of a lineup later.

item.title: You ignore obvious errors when your mind is focused.
item.description: In a 1981 study, participants frequently failed to notice when researchers asked how many animals of each kind Moses took on the Ark.

item.title: You perceive time as slower when you are afraid.
item.description: A 2007 study demonstrated that participants in high-arousal states, such as bungee jumping, overestimated the duration of temporal intervals.

item.title: Your brain creates a false sense of visual continuity.
item.description: The 'flicker paradigm' reveals that people often fail to notice massive changes in a scene if they occur during a brief flicker.

item.title: You value things more when you think they required effort.
item.description: A 2004 study showed that participants valued the same physical objects more when they were told the creator struggled to make them.

item.title: Your hands and feet influence your perception of distance.
item.description: Reaching with a tool can make objects appear closer than they are, but this is distinct from the 2003 study on physical effort.

item.title: You view your past as a series of constant evolutions.
item.description: A 2013 study found that people report having changed significantly in the past decade but believe they will change little in the future.

item.title: Holding a warm drink makes you judge others as warmer.
item.description: A 2008 study by Williams and Bargh reported this effect, but it has not held up under independent replication.

item.title: You judge people by their actions but yourself by intentions.
item.description: The hypothesis of a foundational actor-observer asymmetry in attribution, while influential in early social psychology, has been largely refuted by meta-analytic evidence.

item.title: You overvalue items because you own them.
item.description: A 1990 study demonstrated that sellers consistently ask for higher prices than buyers are willing to pay for the exact same commodity.

item.title: Testing yourself is a better strategy than studying more.
item.description: The study was published in 'Psychological Science', not 'Perspectives on Psychological Science'.

item.title: You believe that reading is the same as learning.
item.description: Semantic processing results in better recall than structural or phonemic processing, a finding supported by subsequent research that operationalized the theory.

item.title: You are a stranger to your own reasons.
item.description: A 1977 study showed that people often invent plausible, but false, explanations for why they chose one object over another.

item.title: The details you ignore are often the most important ones.
item.description: A 1979 study by Nickerson and Adams showed that people are surprisingly poor at recalling the exact visual details of common objects they encounter daily, such as a penny.

item.title: Your brain groups unrelated information into a single story.
item.description: A 1944 study showed that people reflexively attribute intentional personality traits to simple geometric shapes moving on a screen.

item.title: You view your past habits through an overly optimistic lens.
item.description: The 'false hope syndrome' describes a phenomenon where people fail in their attempts to change because they set unrealistic expectations for the ease and speed of self-change.

item.title: You assume that people act according to their nature.
item.description: The correspondence bias is the tendency to explain behavior as a function of personality rather than the situational constraints.

item.title: You think your past tastes are a map of your future.
item.description: The consistency bias is the tendency to reconstruct your past beliefs to be more in line with your current ones.

item.title: You predict future happiness based on your current physical state.
item.description: The empathy gap describes your inability to understand how your decisions change when you move between a 'hot' state of desire and a 'cold' state of neutrality.

item.title: You struggle to understand that others know what you don't.
item.description: Theory of Mind is a developmental process that matures throughout early childhood, with performance on false-belief tasks typically improving significantly around age four.

item.title: Your expectations of someone actually dictate how they treat you.
item.description: The self-fulfilling prophecy describes how a false definition of a situation evokes behaviors that make the original conception come true.

item.title: You are surprised by the Law of Truly Large Numbers.
item.description: With a large enough sample, many outrageous events are likely to occur.

item.title: You follow successful people even when their methods are flawed.
item.description: Prestige bias is the tendency to copy the behaviors of high-status individuals regardless of whether the behavior contributes to their success.

item.title: You think faces are everywhere because your brain is overactive.
item.description: Pareidolia is the tendency to perceive meaningful patterns, such as faces, in random or ambiguous visual or auditory stimuli.

item.title: You see patterns that do not actually exist in data.
item.description: Apophenia describes the human tendency to perceive meaningful connections between unrelated information.

item.title: You create stories to fill in missing information.
item.description: People consistently invent coherent motives for their random physical actions after the fact.

item.title: You value things more if you had to work for them.
item.description: Increased involvement in the construction of an object leads to a higher subjective appraisal of its worth.

item.title: You stop being curious the moment you name something.
item.description: Labeling an object shifts cognitive focus toward category prototypes at the expense of specific feature recall.

item.title: The first attribute you notice determines your entire assessment.
item.description: The 'primacy effect' in social judgment dictates that initial impressions weight more heavily than subsequent information.

item.title: You judge people by their intent, not their results.
item.description: People perceive harmful actions as less malicious if they believe the actor had a good initial motive.

item.title: You are more honest when you feel observed by eyes.
item.description: A simple image of eyes displayed in a room increases prosocial behavior and honesty in participants.

item.title: Your preferences change based on the choices you ignore.
item.description: Post-decision dissonance reduction causes you to overvalue your chosen option to maintain cognitive consistency.

item.title: You perform worse when you try to consciously control movement.
item.description: Studies on 'choking under pressure' show that focusing on automatic movements impairs skill execution.

item.title: Your brain interprets sound as a visual flash.
item.description: A 2000 study demonstrated that hearing multiple beeps can trick you into seeing a single flash as multiple flashes.

item.title: You ignore the math when certainty is on the table.
item.description: The 'pseudocertainty' effect explains why people choose a certain, smaller gain over a larger, statistically superior gamble.

item.title: You change your mind when you cannot use tools.
item.description: In a 1945 study, participants failed to solve problems because they could not stop seeing an object's 'intended' use.

item.title: You see motion in lights that stay perfectly still.
item.description: The autokinetic effect was first systematically applied in psychology by Muzafer Sherif in 1935 to study social norms, though the phenomenon was documented by astronomers much earlier.

item.title: You judge powerful people based on their physical height.
item.description: Research shows that participants consistently associate power-related concepts like 'leader' or 'dominant' with items placed at the top of a screen.

item.title: It is physically harder to look back at things.
item.description: Inhibition of return typically manifests when the interval between a stimulus cue and a target exceeds approximately 300 milliseconds.

item.title: Your attention is limited to one object.
item.description: When you are highly focused on a specific task, you may experience 'inattentional blindness,' where you fail to notice unexpected stimuli in your visual field.

item.title: You assume the person next to you is fine.
item.description: The 'pluralistic ignorance' effect leads individuals to believe they are the only ones struggling while everyone else appears satisfied.

item.title: You overestimate your control over random outcomes.
item.description: When participants in a 1975 study were asked to pick a card, they were more confident of winning if they picked it themselves.
